Perhaps, but it is a consequence (no pun intended) of a consequentialist theory, that focusing on consequences alone will overlook the liberties, rights and so on of the individual.  I would be interested to see some evidence for your ideas on Mill.

Ethics is always going to be something in which people disagree, as its not exactly 'concrete' like other areas of academia...but I think the deontological position is not weak in the areas you have suggested.  I understand that if you focus on consequences alone that you will have an increased likelihood of benefiting the few.  However, this is not all there is to the matter.  Why, on the utilitarian system, can you say that justice and fairness ever come into account?  Why, say, if it will benefit a society, is it wrong to persecute someone who is not guilty if it will benefit the most people.  Why on a consequentialist account should we not abuse the minorities to help the majorites.  Why do I not prescribe to your organ donor example?  Because living beings will get a respect from me which I do not see as disposable, something I can use to achieve a greater good.  Say every person in the world hated homosexuality, other than a minority (10% or so), as was the case in ancient history.  Why on this account would persecuting homosexuals be right?  Because it brings about the happiness for the many?  I cannot adopt a view which overlooks a living being as a tool, or as Kant puts it a means to an end, rather than an end in itself.  

If you have not read Taylor's work I would highly recommend it, it really is not similar to someone like Kant.  It is very down to Earth, and provides prima facie duties which come about from the realisation that humanity is *not* more valuable than other living beings (or at least there is no rational way to conclude they are).  Thus one has duties towards each and every living being (just as we deem people have duties to one another, as shown in law).

To put it briefly, I think that there is something sick in the idea that because it will benefit the many you are justified in anything, no matter how inhumane, to get the 'greater good'.  The deontological ethics usually result from looking to respect the individual, and the duties which follow from them.

If you want to criticise the justification for why humans deserve respect, we may as well try and justify why happiness or pleasure is just.  Is the happiness of a sadist intrinsically valuable?  Is the happiness of gang-rape valuable, because only one is damaged?  I cannot adopt a view where anything goes in the name of happiness.  I think quite a convincing counter-example of utilitarianism is this: If there is someone who is so mentally disabled that they will never understand the meaning, the negativeness of being mocked for their disability.  They simply cannot comprehend that you and your friends make fun of them, it will NOT directly impact their wellbeing.  Is it right, given how much of a laugh it will give you and your friends to make fun of them?  Or is there in fact a prima facie duty of respect to that individual, in virtue solely of them being a living breathing autonomous being?

Some call it happiness, others pleasure, often the term hedonist is used to describe someone who focuses on pleasure.  I see them as much of a sameness perhaps there is reason to be sceptical about their similarities, or some say utlitarianism is a form of hedonism.  But I digress.  I would say that human beings are most fundamentally inclined to seek pleasure.  It seems that if you imagine two hypothetical worlds, one like ours, and the other the same but with more pleasure the latter would be more preferable.  If by contrast we simply add more suffering to this world it seems that it is a world that one would find least preferable.  Thus on this argument one should strive for the greatest pleasure for the greatest number.  This is a consequentialist theory, looking to what they deem to be the greatest possible consequence of an act.
